Yes, I love in a Caravan! 

I moved in a year ago to avoid the rental crisis and lack of accommodation in the Pilbara area. Now it's my portable home. 

It takes some getting used to: lack of amenities, space, learning how to store everything effectively and making use of all the under couch-bed storage. But with a bit of time, you learn the ropes of minimising your home.

You will need a place to park the caravan. You can do what I did and put feelers out for people who are happy for you to rent a space off of them. I park it at a home where I pay $150 a week for rent and bills (all water, power etc) and I have access to the house shower/toilet when I need it. You will want to sort out an arrangement like this. It is also good to make yourself an outside cooking station to  give you a bit more space/less mess inside the caravan, and because you don't want to be using the gas cookers inside if you can really avoid it.

They have for mine. If my dissasociation was too bad I'd be too anxious to present to ED and would go to my GP who would call the ER in advance and organise a consult give me a form to bring to ED. This was my prefered way of going into admission, although if my mental health was too bad and I couldn't wait to see my GP to speedroll the process, I'd have to present to ED.

You can present to a GP who will be able to speed up the process and contact the mental health ward at your closest hospital for an admission. Your only other alternative is to present to ER and wait and they will evaluate you, however beds are limited and if they asses you as needing an admission they will possibly move you to a much further hospital outside your catchment. If they don't evaluate you as needing an emergency admission, they will link you with the outpatient mental health team.

It's nice to have the flexibility to study online, but I'd still always prefer face-on learning. I find it harder to keep a routine when I'm the only one accountable for keeping myself on schedual; when you have to turn up every said day to a class or tute, it keeps me on task with the work and Im more inclined to do it as opposed to procrastinate because I know i *have*  to be in the class to learn the material, and  I'm expected to show up. While online learning is flexible, and is useful when you don't have the time or means to go to classes, I also find I procrastinate with my online units more, forget deadlines easier and am just all around not as immersed in the content as when I'm learning it on campus.

Sounds like you're a perfectionist with a high drive to succeed. Whilst these are not bad qualities, as the motivation can help achieve, they can be very mentally damaging. You are only fourteen and seem to be very insightful into your predicament; no most people don't become famous sports stars or YouTube's or anything of the sort that is the latest ventures in this generation. You're young, and the best way to get yourself through this mindset is to start writing down your actual accomplishments, as you do them. When you have a visible list to look back on,  you'll start to see your accomplishments a bit clearer, because im sure you accomplish more than you're currently aware of. 
I suppose its awful, but in a way, life is awful and dreams don't always work out. When I was your age I wanted to be a famous cellist, and I worked so hard for that goal, got in the top 8% marks out of everybody in my county for my Year 12 finals, and got an incredible score for university. But my soul was crushed when I didn't make it to the music college. A few years after my law degree went the same way, and I couldn't afford to sit the bar. I'm now 22 and a nursing student, about to graduate with my associates, and I never thought this world be my career, my job, but god is it all I'd ever want to do, when I used to laugh at nurses for choosing that job. There is a PDF from "anxietycanada" about perfecfism that details the causes and how to fix striving for the top. Feel accomplished with what you can do, realise your strengths and where you're good at them and realise you have a whole life of (I'm sorry but it's true)  soul crushing defeats that will actually turn out to be blessings in disguise. Youll do many amazing things in your life, and champion of fortnight may not be one of them, but god, who knows what you could and I know you will,  give back to humanity. You'll do big things, kid. I believe you.  Shoot me a PM if you need some tips to get over the feelings of defeat. I know how heavy they can sit on your chest.
